meetings.title: City council — closed procurement review
meetings.memo:
Closed session. Their DPO sat in the back and stayed silent until minute forty.

Highlight of the demo: I unplugged the Wi‑Fi and transcription kept running — Tom actually clapped. Marieke needs every claim in writing for the DPIA. Tom's pain point is renaming speakers after the fact; clerks constantly merge the wrong councillor with the wrong agenda item.

Before Friday: security one-pager, installer SHA-256, and a Word export with speaker labels on the annex debate.

transcript.speaker: Marieke
transcript.text: Our DPO will ask where the models live, who updates them, and whether a single byte of audio leaves this laptop during summarization.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Models sit in app storage after download. Summaries and chat run locally. The only network call is optional — signing in on the website if you want team invites.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: We tried another vendor last year. The moment we saw “uploading audio” we killed the pilot. Can clerks fix speaker names after the meeting?

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Rename once and it propagates through the transcript and every export. I'll generate a DOCX with your annex headings before we leave.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: What if I pull the network cable mid-meeting — does it keep up with De Vries when he goes off-script for twenty minutes?

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Want to see? I'll kill Wi‑Fi right now.

transcript.speaker: Marieke
transcript.text: …It actually continued. Fine. Send the written guarantees and we'll schedule a pilot with planning committee recordings.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: And add a line in the docs about merging speakers — that's the feature that'll save my team hours.

meetings.title: Hospital admins — field interview synthesis
meetings.memo:
Merged three interviews with ICU administrators and a privacy officer. Same story every time: they want AI notes, compliance says no cloud.

Dr. Weiss literally said “we cannot have patient names on someone else's GPU.” Elena proved the meeting chat could answer “what did everyone disagree on?” across a ninety-minute file without sending anything upstream.

Product takeaway: speaker labels in Word exports matter more than fancy UI — five of six participants said that's what they email to legal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Weiss
transcript.text: We have residents recording handoffs on their phones because the official tool uploads to Virginia. That is not happening on my ward.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: When I diarized yesterday's interview, it thought the participant was two people until minute twelve. Took me thirty seconds to merge — acceptable?

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Click the speaker name, assign all segments, done. No re-upload, no waiting on a server.

transcript.speaker: James
transcript.text: My question is exports. Legal wants Word with speaker names, not a screenshot of your app.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: DOCX export is local too — same labels you see in the transcript tab.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: I asked the chat who pushed back on the budget — it quoted three moments across Dutch and English without me scrubbing the file manually.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Weiss
transcript.text: If you can prove the audio never leaves the machine, I'll champion a pilot with three department heads.

transcript.speaker: James
transcript.text: Send me the data-flow diagram. If it's accurate, privacy review moves from months to weeks.

meetings.title: Investor dry run — confidential
meetings.memo:
Confidential. Practised the deck out loud; recording caught me rambling on enterprise pricing for four minutes straight.

Sarah from Horizon pushed hard: “What stops Microsoft from adding this?” Answer: regulated buyers who need proof audio never left the device. Marcus wants GDPR-by-design as a full slide, not a footnote.

Board decision: lead with the municipality win, live demo only, no cloud backup story.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Walk me through the worst case. A clerk records a closed session — where does that file go?

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: SQLite on their laptop. We never receive the audio. Team features are metadata only — seats, invites, org name.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So your moat is compliance, not model quality. What stops Microsoft from shipping the same thing?

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Their business model assumes cloud. Our buyers ask for air-gapped workflows — councils, hospitals, law firms.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Put GDPR-by-design on its own slide. Investors will probe data residency in the first five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Chair
transcript.text: Ninety-second product moment. Live transcription beats another architecture diagram.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: I'll record tonight's run-through, tighten the summary, and paste action items into the board memo — all local.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: If the municipality pilot converts, we'll talk about leading the round. Don't send me a cloud link.

meetings.title: Trade show demo — post-mortem
meetings.memo:
The Hannover demo crashed in front of forty people because the model download hadn't finished on hotel Wi‑Fi.

Sales improvised — opened an existing meeting and showed summary + chat instead. Audience laughed, client booked a follow-up anyway.

Lesson: never trust conference Wi‑Fi. Ship a “demo mode” bundle pre-loaded; add installer size to the changelog mirror so support stops guessing.

transcript.speaker: Sales
transcript.text: Forty people staring at a progress bar that said twelve percent for six minutes. I aged five years.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: Post-recording diarization is solid on hour-long files now — shame nobody saw it live.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: I opened yesterday's council recording, ran summary, asked chat what objections came up — crowd actually leaned in.

transcript.speaker: Design
transcript.text: People couldn't find regenerate summary. If we'd had that on the dock, recovery would've looked intentional.

transcript.speaker: Sales
transcript.text: The procurement lead still booked Tuesday. Said “if it works offline, we need it.”

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: I'll add a demo bundle and a green “models ready” gate that blocks record until download completes.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Marketing gets the hero preview updated to show the real tabs — no more fake play button moments.

items.question: Is MeetingRoom suitable for GDPR and sensitive data?
items.answer: MeetingRoom is designed to help organizations that must protect personal and confidential information. Because meeting audio and AI processing stay on your devices, you avoid sending meeting content to third-party cloud AI providers. That supports common GDPR goals such as limiting transfers, reducing subprocessors for meeting data, and keeping control over retention. Your organization remains responsible for its own GDPR compliance — but local-first processing removes a major source of risk compared to cloud-only meeting tools.

items.question: Is my data stored locally?
items.answer: Yes, 100%. MeetingRoom processes everything on your device. Your audio, transcripts, and summaries never leave your machine. There are no cloud servers involved in processing your data.

items.question: What platforms are supported?
items.answer: MeetingRoom runs on Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit / x64) and macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 chip or newer). Intel Macs, 32-bit Windows, and Linux are not supported.

items.question: What are the system requirements?
items.answer: You need Windows 10/11 (64-bit) or macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 or newer), plus at least 8GB of RAM. For the best AI performance, 16GB of RAM is recommended.

items.question: How does the license work?
items.answer: Personal licenses are per-user. Team licenses are per-seat with centralized billing. You can manage your subscription and seats through the Paddle customer portal.

items.question: Does it need internet?
items.answer: Only for the initial download of AI models (a one-time setup). After that, MeetingRoom works completely offline. No internet connection is needed for recording, transcription, or summarization.

items.question: What languages does it support?
items.answer: MeetingRoom supports Dutch, English, French, German, and Spanish — both for the user interface and for AI transcription and summaries.

documentation.headline: Documentation
documentation.intro: Install MeetingRoom on a supported platform and get productive with local AI meeting notes.

sections.title: Supported platforms
sections.body:
MeetingRoom runs on Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit / x64) and macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 chip or newer).

Intel-based Macs, 32-bit Windows, and Linux are not supported.

sections.title: Installation (Windows x64)
sections.body:
Requires Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit (x64).

Download the installer from the changelog on our website. Run the setup wizard and choose an install location with enough disk space for AI models (several gigabytes).

If Windows SmartScreen appears, choose “More info” and “Run anyway” only if you trust the publisher (Innovolabs).

sections.title: Installation (Apple Silicon Mac)
sections.body:
Requires a Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 chip or newer). Intel Macs are not supported.

Download the disk image (.dmg) from the changelog on our website. Open it and drag MeetingRoom into Applications.

On first launch, macOS may ask you to confirm that you want to open an app from Innovolabs. If Gatekeeper blocks the app, open System Settings → Privacy & Security and choose “Open Anyway” only if you trust the publisher.

sections.title: First launch and models
sections.body:
On first launch, MeetingRoom may download speech and language models to your machine. This step usually requires internet access. After models are installed, transcription and summarization work fully offline.

You can manage storage from in-app settings when available.

sections.title: Recording and exporting
sections.body:
Start a new meeting recording from the main screen. Use a clear microphone placement for best diarization.

Export transcripts and summaries to PDF or Word when your license includes export features. All content remains on your device unless you choose to copy it elsewhere.

sections.title: Languages and troubleshooting
sections.body:
MeetingRoom supports Dutch, English, French, German, and Spanish in the UI and for AI output.

If transcription is slow, close other heavy applications, ensure you are on AC power on laptops, and check that models finished downloading. For persistent issues, contact support with your app version from the changelog page.

meta.description: How MeetingRoom treats your data with local-first processing.

privacy.headline: Privacy Policy
privacy.disclaimer: This policy is provided for general information. It is not legal advice. Ask qualified counsel to align it with your regulatory context.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: MeetingRoom is built so that meeting audio, transcripts, and AI-generated notes are processed and stored on your own devices. We do not operate a cloud service that processes your meeting content on our servers in the same way many online meeting assistants do.

sections.title: What we may collect
sections.body:
When you purchase a license, our payment provider (for example Paddle) processes billing data according to their own privacy policy. The website may collect standard technical logs that hosting providers typically keep (such as IP address and browser type) for security and reliability.

The MeetingRoom desktop application itself is designed to keep your meeting material local.

sections.title: Local processing
sections.body: AI transcription, summarization, and chat features run on your hardware after models are installed. You should still protect device access with passwords, disk encryption, and your organization’s policies.

sections.title: Retention and your choices
sections.body: You control how long recordings and notes remain on disk. Uninstalling the application or deleting local data files removes that content from the device, subject to your operating system and backup tools.

sections.title: Contact
sections.body: Questions about this policy or privacy practices can be sent to the addresses listed on the Contact page.
